candidates.title: The girl from the park, six years later
candidates.detail: Shannon Hayes is in this episode's guest cast, and one of the players recruited at the open trials is called Shannon. Hayes has played the character since season one's second episode, 'Biscuits' (2020), credited then simply as 'Soccer Girl' — the kid Ted keeps running into playing football near his flat, who gives him sass and beats the boys in her school uniform. If the recruit is her, a throwaway street-corner character planted in the show's second-ever episode has just made a professional squad. candidates.title: Losing a striker to pregnancy is a rules story, not just a plot
candidates.detail: The squad loses a striker to pregnancy leave, which is what forces the open trials. The real-world backdrop: FIFA only wrote maternity protection into the Regulations on the Status and Transfer of Players in 2020, in force from 1 January 2021 — a minimum of 14 weeks' paid leave at no less than two thirds of salary, at least eight of those weeks after the birth, and sanctions for a club that terminates a contract over a pregnancy. The protections were extended to female coaches in 2024. Within living memory of the sport, the plot of this episode would have ended a career rather than opened a trial.
candidates.moment: Early in the episode, when a player learns she is pregnant and the coaches face a hole in the squad.

candidates.title: The centre back brings her son to the trial
candidates.detail: Lizzie Davis turns up to the open trial as a single mother who could not find childcare, so she brings her boy with her. The recap reads it as proof of how much she wants it. It is also the episode being specific about the everyday obstacle that keeps women out of the semi-professional game — not talent, logistics.

candidates.title: Dani Rojas's sister is played by Cristo Fernandez's actual sister
candidates.detail: Maria Rojas auditions at the open trials. She is played by Paloma Cinco, who is Cristo Fernandez's real-life sister — and according to the episode's production notes the two of them pitched the idea together. Her character cannot really play, and is at peace with a life that is not football, which is a quiet joke at the expense of her screen brother's entire personality.

candidates.title: Henry is played by a new actor, and football is the reason
candidates.detail: Henry arrives in London and starts school here. He is played by Grant Feely, who took over from Gus Turner between seasons — reported by Deadline in March 2025. The stated reason is practical rather than dramatic: Henry's football is now front and centre, so the part needed a child actor who could actually play. Feely had previously played the young Luke Skywalker in Obi-Wan Kenobi.

candidates.title: Rebecca's pitch is about the boys watching
candidates.detail: Selling the women's team to sponsors, Rebecca does not argue fairness. She argues that funding it changes what the next generation of boys grows up expecting to see as normal. It is the same structure as her season-one arc in reverse — using the club as an instrument, but now for something worth building.

candidates.title: The obstacle is being taken seriously, not being good
candidates.detail: Every recap converges on the same throughline: Richmond's hard problem this week is not assembling a competent side, it is persuading sponsors, press and the club itself that the women's team is worth taking seriously. The trials, the financial reports and Rebecca's pitch are three angles on one argument.
